evidence.title: Ten-year analysis of 17,639 thoracolumbar instrumentation failures using the manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database.
evidence.abstract: Background This study utilized the FDA-maintained Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database, an extensive resource capturing medical device reports (MDRs) of adverse events, to perform a cross-sectional analysis of failure mechanisms reported by manufacturers. Methods All thoracolumbar pedicle screw system failures reported in the MAUDE database between January 2014 and December 2023 were identified using FDA product codes. Failures were classified as intraoperative or postoperative and grouped into 9 and 5 clusters, respectively. Following de-identification, the 8 most frequently reported manufacturers were analyzed individually. Reports specifying failed components were categorized as screw, set screw, rod, instrument, system, other, or unknown. The "system failure" category lacked specificity regarding the failed component. Descriptive statistics summarized failure mechanisms. Results A total of 17,639 MDRs related to thoracolumbar fixation failures were reported over the past decade, with 15,234 postoperative and 2,405 intraoperative events. The most frequent intraoperative issues were positioning problems (27.9%), device-device compatibility (26.4%), and difficulty in separation/removal (11.8%), while the most common postoperative failure mechanisms were breakage (45.2%), migration/detachment (42%), and deformation (10.1%). The distribution of failed components varied by the associated failure mechanism. Among 4,676 reported breakages, screws (20.8%), set screws (15.5%), and rods (11.8%) were most frequently involved. In the 4,871 migration/detachment events, set screws accounted for 31.6%, screws for 21%, and rods for 2.3%. Of 1,325 deformation events, the majority were linked to set screws (76.5%), with fewer attributed to system-level components (11.2%) and screws (6%). Conclusions Failure profiles for pedicle screw systems vary significantly between manufacturers. The MAUDE database is a useful resource for the evaluation of reportin

evidence.title: Management of neurologically intact traumatic posterior atlantoaxial dislocation with odontoid fracture and bilateral locked facets: a case report and literature review.
evidence.abstract: Background Traumatic posterior atlantoaxial dislocation (TPAD) with an associated odontoid fracture is exceedingly rare, typically resulting from high-energy trauma such as high-velocity road traffic accidents or falls from height. This report details a previously undescribed case of an old TPAD combined with a Type II odontoid fracture and bilateral locked facets in a patient who remained neurologically intact. We also systematically review the literature on the diagnosis and management of this injury pattern to provide evidence-based guidance for clinical decisions. Case presentation A 67-year-old woman presented with significant neck pain and stiffness, but no neurological deficit, following a traffic accident. After four years of failed conservative management, she underwent posterior release, reduction, and screw-rod fixation. Postoperatively and throughout follow-up, she experienced complete resolution of symptoms and demonstrated improved alignment on imaging, with no intraoperative or postoperative complications. Conclusions The surgical management of old dislocation with bilateral locked facets presents substantial technical challenges. For this specific type of TPAD, a single posterior approach incorporating facet release, reduction, and screw-rod fixation represents an effective and safe option, achieving satisfactory clinical outcomes.

evidence.title: Minimally invasive lateral tubular approach for revision of failed lumbar interbody fusion: illustrative cases.
evidence.abstract: Background Interbody cage failure is associated with loss of disc height, nerve compression, and pseudarthrosis, and often requires reoperation. Revision of failed interbody cages is challenging due to subsidence of the cage into the adjacent endplates, causing bony defects and granulation tissue, resulting in difficult exposure and a higher risk of complications. Observations In this case series, the authors present 2 cases of symptomatic interbody cage failure successfully revised using a minimally invasive lateral approach. The first case utilized a transpsoas lateral approach to replace a failed L2-3 cage from prior transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion. The second case used an anterior-to-psoas oblique lateral approach to revise a subsided L3 corpectomy cage. Postoperatively, both patients had significant symptom improvement. Lessons A lateral lumbar interbody approach-with its direct access to disc space, possibility for a relatively large-footprint cage while avoiding scar tissue from a prior approach, and favorable safety profile-is a promising option for the revision of failed interbody cages. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE25750.

evidence.title: Enhancing C2 pedicle screw placement in Hangman's fractures: a comparative study of navigation and 3D printed guidance techniques.
evidence.abstract: Objective This retrospective study aimed to analyze the accuracy and safety of pedicle screw placement in upper cervical spine surgery for Hangman's fractures, particularly in cases with high-riding vertebral artery (HRVA) at C2, using navigation technology and 3D-printed patient-specific templates. Methods We included 33 patients with Hangman's fractures who underwent posterior cervical fixation with bone graft fusion or non-bone graft fusion surgery between January 2013 and January 2023. Patients were divided into two groups based on the intraoperative pedicle screw placement method: Group A ( n = 15) utilized a navigation system, and Group B ( n = 18) used a 3D printed navigation template. Clinical and radiological data were collected and compared. Results One hundred and forty-four screws (66 navigated, 78 3D-printed templates) were inserted without vertebral artery, spinal cord, or nerve injury. Operative time per screw: Group A 24.0 ± 5.6 min vs. Group B 18.7 ± 4.1 min; mean difference 5.3 min (22% reduction; 95% CI -9.1 to -1.5; P = 0.018). Intra-operative blood loss:152 ± 29 ml vs. 105 ± 19 mL; mean difference 47 mL (95% CI -66 to -19; P = 0.001). Overall accuracy (Grade 0 + 1) was 98.5% (65/66) vs. 98.7% (77/78) (odds ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.11-10.2; P = 0.97). In the Type-III fracture subgroup (8 screws per group), templates achieved 100% accuracy vs. 87.5% with navigation ( P = 0.032) and lower cortical penetration (12.5% vs. 37.5%; P = 0.008). Post-operative VAS and NDI improved comparably (all inter-group P > 0.05). At 24-month follow-up, all fractures had healed; C2/3 fusion rates did not differ (facet fusion 100% vs. 100%; inter-body fusion 39% vs. 39%; P > 0.99). Conclusion The use of 3D-printed patient-specific templates in upper cervical spine surgery for Hangman's fractures, especially in the presence of HRVA, is effective and safe. evidence.title: The Role of Robot-Assisted Technique in Treating Adult Degenerative Scoliosis with Circumferential Minimal Invasive Correction Surgery - A Retrospective Analysis of 51 Consecutive Cases.
evidence.abstract: Study design Retrospective chart review. Objective This study aims to investigate the application of robots in treating adult degenerative scoliosis (ADS) with circumferential minimal invasive surgery (cMIS). Background The cMIS is useful but faces a lot of challenges in correcting ADS. One of the most important challenges is the difficulty in screw placement. Robot-assisted technique demonstrates lots of advantages but the data about its application in treating ADS is limited in literatures. Methods A total of 51 cases diagnosed with ADS were retrospectively analyzed. All patients underwent cMIS technique with staged surgeries (OLIF and PPS fixation). Group A enrolled 21 patients and performed robot-assisted technique. Group B enrolled 30 patients and performed fluoroscopy guided technique. Clinical outcomes like the operation time, radiation exposure, pressure curve and post-operation VAS score were recorded. 3D-CT scan was also performed to evaluate the accuracy of the screws. warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

Any anti-fouling mechanism that relies on flow direction must be tested against RETROGRADE flow. Retrograde flow is a realistic clinical scenario (cough, Valsalva, venous pressure changes).

ALWAYS report worst-case reliability for clinical devices. Averages mask catastrophic failure modes. Thermal activation in a 37°C body environment has a narrow window (37-45°C = 8°C max). Sensor electronics are a SPOF that cannot be fully resolved by redundancy (common-mode failures).

informational.lesson: Do not assume VP shunt problems apply to the eShunt. The eShunt's drainage geometry is fundamentally different (short path, no siphon). Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

Methods All thoracolumbar pedicle screw system failures reported in the MAUDE database between January 2014 and December 2023 were identified using FDA product codes. Failures were classified as intraoperative or postoperative and grouped into 9 and 5 clusters, respectively. Following de-identification, the 8 most frequently reported manufacturers were analyzed individually. Reports specifying failed components were categorized as screw, set screw, rod, instrument, system, other, or unknown. The "system failure" category lacked specificity regarding the failed component. Descriptive statistics summarized failure mechanisms. Results A total of 17,639 MDRs related to thoracolumbar fixation failures were reported over the past decade, with 15,234 postoperative and 2,405 intraoperative events. The most frequent intraoperative issues were positioning problems (27.9%), device-device compatibility (26.4%), and difficulty in separation/removal (11.8%), while the most common postoperative failure mechanisms were breakage (45.2%), migration/detachment (42%), and deformation (10.1%). The distribution of failed components varied by the associated failure mechanism. Among 4,676 reported breakages, screws (20.8%), set screws (15.5%), and rods (11.8%) were most frequently involved. In the 4,871 migration/detachment events, set screws accounted for 31.6%, screws for 21%, and rods for 2.3%. Of 1,325 deformation events, the majority were linked to set screws (76.5%), with fewer attributed to system-level components (11.2%) and screws (6%). custody_records.raw_content: Background Traumatic posterior atlantoaxial dislocation (TPAD) with an associated odontoid fracture is exceedingly rare, typically resulting from high-energy trauma such as high-velocity road traffic accidents or falls from height. This report details a previously undescribed case of an old TPAD combined with a Type II odontoid fracture and bilateral locked facets in a patient who remained neurologically intact. We also systematically review the literature on the diagnosis and management of this injury pattern to provide evidence-based guidance for clinical decisions. Case presentation A 67-year-old woman presented with significant neck pain and stiffness, but no neurological deficit, following a traffic accident. After four years of failed conservative management, she underwent posterior release, reduction, and screw-rod fixation. Postoperatively and throughout follow-up, she experienced complete resolution of symptoms and demonstrated improved alignment on imaging, with no intraoperative or postoperative complications. Conclusions The surgical management of old dislocation with bilateral locked facets presents substantial technical challenges. For this specific type of TPAD, a single posterior approach incorporating facet release, reduction, and screw-rod fixation represents an effective and safe option, achieving satisfactory clinical outcomes.

custody_records.raw_content: Background Interbody cage failure is associated with loss of disc height, nerve compression, and pseudarthrosis, and often requires reoperation. Revision of failed interbody cages is challenging due to subsidence of the cage into the adjacent endplates, causing bony defects and granulation tissue, resulting in difficult exposure and a higher risk of complications. Observations In this case series, the authors present 2 cases of symptomatic interbody cage failure successfully revised using a minimally invasive lateral approach. The first case utilized a transpsoas lateral approach to replace a failed L2-3 cage from prior transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion. The second case used an anterior-to-psoas oblique lateral approach to revise a subsided L3 corpectomy cage. Postoperatively, both patients had significant symptom improvement. Lessons A lateral lumbar interbody approach-with its direct access to disc space, possibility for a relatively large-footprint cage while avoiding scar tissue from a prior approach, and favorable safety profile-is a promising option for the revision of failed interbody cages. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE25750.

custody_records.raw_content: Objective This retrospective study aimed to analyze the accuracy and safety of pedicle screw placement in upper cervical spine surgery for Hangman's fractures, particularly in cases with high-riding vertebral artery (HRVA) at C2, using navigation technology and 3D-printed patient-specific templates. Methods We included 33 patients with Hangman's fractures who underwent posterior cervical fixation with bone graft fusion or non-bone graft fusion surgery between January 2013 and January 2023. Patients were divided into two groups based on the intraoperative pedicle screw placement method: Group A ( n = 15) utilized a navigation system, and Group B ( n = 18) used a 3D printed navigation template. Clinical and radiological data were collected and compared. Results One hundred and forty-four screws (66 navigated, 78 3D-printed templates) were inserted without vertebral artery, spinal cord, or nerve injury. Operative time per screw: Group A 24.0 ± 5.6 min vs. Group B 18.7 ± 4.1 min; mean difference 5.3 min (22% reduction; 95% CI -9.1 to -1.5; P = 0.018). Intra-operative blood loss:152 ± 29 ml vs. 105 ± 19 mL; mean difference 47 mL (95% CI -66 to -19; P = 0.001). Overall accuracy (Grade 0 + 1) was 98.5% (65/66) vs. 98.7% (77/78) (odds ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.11-10.2; P = 0.97). In the Type-III fracture subgroup (8 screws per group), templates achieved 100% accuracy vs. 87.5% with navigation ( P = 0.032) and lower cortical penetration (12.5% vs. 37.5%; P = 0.008). Post-operative VAS and NDI improved comparably (all inter-group P > 0.05). At 24-month follow-up, all fractures had healed; C2/3 fusion rates did not differ (facet fusion 100% vs. 100%; inter-body fusion 39% vs. 39%; P > 0.99). Conclusion The use of 3D-printed patient-specific templates in upper cervical spine surgery for Hangman's fractures, especially in the presence of HRVA, is effective and safe. Objective This study aims to investigate the application of robots in treating adult degenerative scoliosis (ADS) with circumferential minimal invasive surgery (cMIS). Background The cMIS is useful but faces a lot of challenges in correcting ADS. One of the most important challenges is the difficulty in screw placement. Robot-assisted technique demonstrates lots of advantages but the data about its application in treating ADS is limited in literatures. Methods A total of 51 cases diagnosed with ADS were retrospectively analyzed. All patients underwent cMIS technique with staged surgeries (OLIF and PPS fixation). Group A enrolled 21 patients and performed robot-assisted technique. Group B enrolled 30 patients and performed fluoroscopy guided technique. Clinical outcomes like the operation time, radiation exposure, pressure curve and post-operation VAS score were recorded. 3D-CT scan was also performed to evaluate the accuracy of the screws.
